Introduction Modern software development increasingly embraces multilingual pro- gramming, allowingdeveloperstoleveragethestrengthsofmultipleprogram- minglanguageswithinasingleproject (Yangetal.,2024;Mayeretal.,2017; Lietal.,2024;Kochhar et al.,2016). Atthecore ofmultilingualdevelopment lies the Foreign Function Interface (FFI), which enables seamless integration and mutual calls between languages. Many traditional programming lan- guages provide FFIs to support cross-language interoperability, such as the Python/C API in Python (Python, 2009), JNI in Java (Oracle, 2017) and FFI-NAPI in JavaScript (Henningsen, 2017). These FFIs greatly boost de- velopment efficiency by allowing code reuse, expanding application scenarios, and supporting the creation of more efficient, powerful, and scalable software systems. Goprogramminglanguage(Golang),whichhasseensignificantgrowth(Jet- Brains, 2021) and reached 7th place in the TOBIE index (TIOBE, 2024) in December 2024, offers a unique FFI called CGO. CGO allows direct inter- action between Go and C, combining Go’s simplicity and efficiency with C’s power and maturity. This makes CGO invaluable in areas like system-level programming and performance-critical tasks. With widespread applications of Golang (JetBrains, 2021), popular Go projects like Docker (Hykes and Docker, 2013) and Go-Ethereum (Foundation, 2014), which leverage CGO, are now widely used around the world. While FFIs like CGO offer significant advantages in software develop- ment, they also introduce challenges. Research (Li et al., 2023, 2022; Grichi etal.,2020;Mayeretal.,2017)showsthatdifferencesinlanguagefeaturesbe- tween programming languages—such as memory management, type systems, exception handling, and concurrency mechanisms—can make cross-language programming more complex, increasing risks in the interface layer. These risks include performance overhead, difficult debugging, and potential secu- rity vulnerabilities, etc. (Li et al., 2023). To mitigate these risks, understanding the distribution, patterns, pur- poses, and critical issues of cross-language is essential for building efficient 2 and secure multilingual systems. Identifying common use cases and pain pointscanhelpdevelopersproposebettersolutions. Whilemuchresearchhas focusedontraditionalPython/C(HuandZhang,2020,2023)andJNI(Grichi et al., 2020; Hwang et al., 2024), there has been limited study on CGO. Previous studies offer valuable insights, but their findings to other FFIs are not applicable to CGO due to Go’s unique design philosophy and runtime characteristics. Unlike Python or Java, Go compiles programs ahead of time and has simpler language features. Go is a statically-compiled language that avoids using a virtual machine, features a simple syntax, and includes a runtime with built-in concurrency support and other advanced capabilities, settingitapartfromJavaandPython. Go’scomplexandrichruntimesystem and CGO’s seamless integration with Go’s tooling and runtime strengthen the language’s distinctiveness. CGO’s close coupling with Go allows direct interaction with C code through a pseudo-package (named C), simplifying development but introduc- ing unique challenges. For example, Go’s garbage collector manages memory automatically, while C requires manual memory management. This discrep- ancy can lead to memory issues such as dangling references and memory leaks, since Go may not recognize memory allocated and referenced by C. To mitigate such memory issues, Go imposes certain restrictions on the use of CGO, such as not allowing Go code to store Go pointers in C mem- ory (Google, 2022c). These restrictions require Go to perform checks during compilation or runtime, which may lead to false positives. For instance, Go’s issue#63460 (Teo, 2023) mentions that the current CGO checks may falsely report issues when encountering a struct containing a Go pointer, causing a normal program to crash. Additionally, these complexities make develop- ment more cumbersome and error-prone due to the intricacies of type and data conversions and the need to track reference relationships. For instance, in issue#200 (Simon Place, 2017) of repository glfw, the developer’s lack of understanding regarding CGO restrictions and patterns led to incorrect usage, resulting in a runtime panic. Despite CGO’s unique characteristics, which may introduce additional challenges and issues, currently, there is a lack of comprehensive study on CGO usage. This gap leaves both Go team and developers ill-equipped to handle its complexities, potentially leading to the runtime errors mentioned above, as well as other avoidable pitfalls such as inefficient code and longer debugging times.The lack of targeted research also hinders the development of tools and best practices for CGO, limiting its adoption and effectiveness. 3 To address the research gap and provide developers with a comprehensive understanding of CGO, we conduct an empirical study of CGO usage in popular open-source Go projects on GitHub. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to reveal the distribution, purposes, patterns, and critical issues associated with CGO, while also proposing solutions to address these identified critical issues. Our findings provide valuable insights for Go developers and the Go team, helping to improve CGO usage and its integration in Go projects. We developed a tool named CGOAnalyzer to identify and quantify CGO features in Go projects, offering detailed insights into CGO usage. By lever- aging CGOAnalyzer, we gain a thorough understanding of CGO usage in open-source Go projects. We examine the purposes behind CGO adoption, analyze common usage patterns, and identify potential critical risks it may pose to Go projects, while also proposing solutions to mitigate these risks. Our study is guided by four research questions (RQs): the first three RQs focus on the distribution, purposes, patterns, and common issues, while RQ4 investigates the root causes and solutions for the critical issues identified. The findings from these RQs can help developers write more efficient, safe code and provide valuable insights to the Go team for enhancing the safety of CGO and improving the toolchain robustness. In summary, we have made the following contributions: 1) Development of CGOAnalyzer. We developed CGOAnalyzer, a tool for identifying and quantifying CGO-related language features in Go projects. It retrieves the top 1,000 most-starred Go repositories via the GitHub API, collects CGO-related issues and commits, and performs static analysis on their ASTs to extract relevant features such as function calls. We also identify 3 purposes (§4.1), 15 usage patterns (Table 5), and 5 common issue categories (§4.3). Notably, false positive runtime crashes caused by CGO’s unnecessary pointer checks emerge as a critical issue. 3) Study on Critical CGO Pointer-Check Related Issues. These fundamental differences in usage mean that previous studies on usage statistics, patterns, or other factors for the Python/C API, JNI, or other FFIs may not directly apply to CGO. The streamlined integration and distinct usage of CGO result in unique usage characteristics that require independent study. 2.1.2. Unique Restriction CGO enables mutual function calls between Go and C, allowing Go’s runtime components, such as the garbage collector, memory allocator, and goroutinescheduler,tocoexistwithCduringexecution. Toensuretheproper functioning of Go’s runtime components, such as the garbage collector, Go imposes certain restrictions that developers must follow when passing point- ers between Go and C using CGO (Google, 2022c). For example, Go code is not allowed to pass any pointers that point to Go memory containing Go pointer, nor to store Go pointers in C memory. These restrictions can be checked dynamically at runtime by the function cgoCheckPointer inserted by the Go compilation toolchain. Moreover, due to the differing runtime management systems of Go and C, developers must comply with certain implicit restrictions to ensure the proper functioning of programs. For example, since Go manages memory using a garbage collector while C relies on manual management, interactions betweenGoandCviaCGOcanresultinmemoryissueslikedanglingpointers and memory leaks, as the Go runtime cannot recognize memory allocations and references in C. Such restrictions require developers to redesign data representations and adapt third-party libraries, involving complex type and data conversions, as well as the maintenance and tracking of reference relationships when using CGO. This makes the code more cumbersome and error-prone, creating chal- lenges that are not present in well-established interfaces like the Python/C API or JNI. Unfortunately, there is currently no dedicated study on CGO, leaving developers unaware of its restrictions. This can have a negative impact on 7 development, both in terms of efficiency and reliability. For instance, in issue#200 (Simon Place, 2017) of repository glfw, the developer’s lack of understandingregardingCGOrestrictionsandpatternsledtoincorrectusage of CGO, causing the program to panic during runtime. Therefore, To make developers aware of these explicit and implicit re- strictions, and to identify the best development practices that can enhance both efficiency and reliability, a comprehensive study of the current CGO usage patterns and issues is necessary. 2.1.3. Unique Process Flow For CGO programs, the Go compilation toolchain performs additional preprocessing steps. It rewrites the original CGO calls to generate multiple intermediatefiles, whicharethencompiledalongwiththerestoftheprogram during the compilation stage. During this process, the default C compiler (usually GCC) is invoked to handle the compilation of the C code. This is in contrast to Python/C API and JNI, where the source code typically doesn’t require such preprocessing and instead focuses on runtime bindings. CGO directly integrates Go and C, managing both the Go and C parts together. Additionally, during runtime, CGO handles challenges like ABI conver- sion, translating data types and calling conventions between the two lan- guages,andstackswitching,seamlesslytransitioningbetweenGostack(Google, 2013) and C stack. It also synchronizes Go’s runtime with C calls to pre- vent conflicts, such as pausing garbage collection when necessary. Unlike Python/C API, which requires manual reference counting and memory man- agement, CGO operates more automatically by integrating closely with the Go runtime. Such unique automatic runtime management ensures that C functions do not disrupt Go’s runtime system. However, there is currently a lack of dedicated studies on CGO, leaving developers without a clear understanding of the potential issues this unique process flow might introduce. Without such understanding, developers may unknowingly implement inefficient or error-prone solutions, which could neg- atively impact development efficiency and reduce the reliability of software. 2.2. Step 2: Retrieve CGO Language Features The CGO language features encompass both utilizing C in Go and in- corporating Go in C. These features can be extracted from the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). Hence, to pinpoint every CGO language feature within a Go project, CGOAnalyzer navigates through the project’s Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to locate them, subsequently documenting them in a database. We use the go/parser (Google, 2022b) package of Go to build standard Go AST from Go source files and use PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL, 2024) as our database. CGOAnalyzer implements an ast.Visitor interface from package go/ast (Google, 2022a) to walk through the Go AST. CGOAnalyzer iden- tifies four categories of CGO language features, corresponding to ❶-❹ in Figure 4, covering both Go-to-C calls and exported Go functions callable by C. 12 ❶ Detection of CGO: CGOAnalyzer inspects each ast.File node in the AST to determine whether the Imports field contains the import "C" direc- tive. Projects with files containing this declaration are classified as utilizing CGO, while those without it are categorized as not using CGO. ❷ Detection of Go-to-C Calls and CGO Type Conversions: In Go, func- tion calls and type conversions are represented as ast.CallExpr nodes in Go AST. CGOAnalyzer analyzes these nodes to identify Go-to-C calls and CGO type conversions. It checks if the node implements the ast.SelectorExpr interface and if the package name in field Sel is C. When the function name matches a predefined list of C type names, the node is classified as a CGO type conversion; otherwise, the node is identified as a Go-to-C function call. ❸ Detection of Exported Go Functions for C-to-Go Calls: Go functions thatarecallablefromCmustbeexplicitlyexported. CGOAnalyzer identifies such functions by inspecting each ast.FuncDecl node for a //export xxx directive in its Doc field. The presence of this directive indicates that the function is exported for C-to-Go interaction. ❹ Detection of Embedded C Code and Compiler Directives: In Go code files utilizing CGO, embedded C code and related directives (e.g., #include for headers and #cgo for C compiler/linker parameters (see Figure 9)) are included in the ast.CommentGroup node of the import "C" statement. Step 3: Find Issues and Commits about CGO CGOAnalyzer utilizes the GitHub API to search for issues and commits related to “CGO” or “C GO” (case insensitive) keywords in those repositories that use CGO identified in Step 2. We manually rule out issues within the golang/go repository, which is the official Go source code repository and issue tracker, as our primary focus is on how CGO is used in open- source repositories rather than the internal development and evolution of CGO within the Go toolchain. Those matched entries are then manually 13 reviewed to identify valuable ones for further analysis of CGO usage and related issues encountered by developers. Finally we obtain 143 valid issues. 3.3. Qualitative Analysis In RQ1 to RQ4, qualitative analysis is sometimes necessary, requiring annotations on certain entries such as files, modules, and issues. To ensure the reliability of the qualitative analysis, we employed the open card-sort method (Fincher and Tenenberg, 2005) for annotation. Initially, both anno- tators independently review and categorize the data, assigning preliminary labels based on observed patterns. When new labels emerged, our authors engaged in discussions to refine and standardize the categories, ensuring con- sistency across annotations. To further validate the annotation process, we assess inter-annotator agreement using the Cohen-Kappa metric (McHugh, 2012), which quanti- fies the level of agreement beyond chance. In cases where discrepancies arise, both annotators conduct follow-up discussions to reconcile differences, refine label definitions, and consolidate the results. This iterative approach helps us maintain annotation accuracy and minimizes subjective bias. Taking the issue analysis in Step 3 as an example, we label issues based on multiple factors, including the issue title, description, subsequent com- ments, and any related pull requests (PRs). Initially, both annotators inde- pendently review each issue to determine its primary category (e.g., issues related to project compilation and build processes). Additional labels are then assigned based on specific details, such as relevant comments or PRs. For instance, if an issue also involves dependency management, it may be given the Dependency label. If an issue spans multiple concerns, we assign multiple labels accordingly. For ambiguous cases, both annotators engaged in further discussion to refine the labeling criteria and reach a consensus. 4. Study on RQ4 - Critical CGO Pointer Check Issues This section provides detailed insights into the critical CGOPointer issues identified in RQ3 (§4.3). We first analyze the root causes of the issues in §5.1. The Root Cause To identify the root cause of the runtime crashes caused by the Go com- pilation toolchain in such critical issues, we analyze cmd/cgo (Google, 2024), the component responsible for handling CGO within the toolchain. As men- tioned in §2.1.2, Go imposes certain restrictions that developers must follow when passing pointers between Go and C using CGO. To ensure these re- strictions are not violated and to maintain the correct execution of the Go runtime, cmd/cgo inserts cgoCheckPointer during CGO preprocessing for potentially suspicious pointers. At runtime, cgoCheckPointer verifies com- pliance with these restrictions and triggers a panic if a violation is detected, terminatingtheprogram. However, thereisagapbetweencurrentimplemen- tation of cmd/cgo and the actual restrictions, causing cmd/cgo to sometimes insert checks for valid pointers, which may lead to false positive panics. Specifically, current cmd/cgo uses a fast yet conservative strategy to de- termine whether to insert cgoCheckPointer for function formal parameters. It checks if the parameter’s type may contain a pointer but does not track or infer the actual argument’s type during CGO preprocessing. The cmd/cgo translates void * in C to unsafe.Pointer in Go. When encountering an ar- gument with a formal parameter type of unsafe.Pointer, cmd/cgo assumes conservatively that the memory pointed to by the argument may contain a pointer. Consequently, it inserts a cgoCheckPointer function call. This be- haviorappliesuniversally: ifaCfunctioncalledbyGohasavoid *pointerin its formal parameter, a cgoCheckPointer will always be inserted, regardless of the actual type pointed to by the argument. mspan is a fundamental memory management unit in Go responsible for managing memory pages. During runtime, function cgoCheckPointer first examines the type of the incoming unsafe.Pointer argument p. If p points to an unknown type, the function then accesses the mspan pointed to by p 29 and searches the entire mspan to see if the Go memory contains a Go pointer. If such a pointer is found, a runtime panic is triggered. 1 ... 2 func main() { 3 var a _Ctype_int = 1 4 func() { _cgo0 := (unsafe.Pointer(&a)); _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil); _Cfunc_print_ptr(_cgo0); }() 5 } Figure 12: Figure 1 after CGO preprocess 1 var p *byte 1 var p *byte 2 p = &b[0] 2 p = &b[0] 3 C.testPtr(unsafe.Pointer(p)) 3 func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(p); _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil); _Cfunc_testPtr(_cgo0); }() Figure 13: Unrecognized ad- dress taken Figure 14: Figure 13 after CGO preprocess The above conservative strategy adopted by cmd/cgo can lead to false positive runtime panics (Cubixmeister, 2016; Per Johansson, 2016; Gernot Vormayr, 2019; tamird, 2018). It may insert checks for valid pointers and trigger a runtime scan of the entire mspan, even when the pointer itself does not violate any restrictions, such as when it points to a Go pointer. However, if the scanned mspan contains any Go pointers, the runtime may mistakenly conclude that the checked pointer also points to a Go pointer, incorrectly identifying a violation and triggering a panic. Taking Figure 1 as an exam- ple, a Go program passes an unsafe.Pointer pointing to an int variable a to C. Though variable a does not contain a pointer, cmd/cgo’s conservative approach still inserts an call to cgoCheckPointer (as shown in Figure 12). This increases the risk of a false positive runtime panic if the mspan contain- ing a includes Go pointers. Furthermore, Go’s issue#18184 (Cubixmeister, 2016) highlights cmd/cgo’s failure to recognize address-taking on a byte slice element, as shown in Figure 13 and Figure 14. Current cmd/cgo cannot de- termine if the unsafe.Pointer points to a slice element and thus inserts a cgoCheckPointer to check the entire mspan, potentially leading to a false positive runtime panic. All in all, the root cause behind these pointer-check-related issues is that the cmd/cgo sometimes cannot figure out what type unsafe.Pointer actually 30 points to. In such cases, cmd/cgo inserts a pointer-check, and Go conser- vatively searches the whole mspan during runtime in the check. To funda- mentally address these issues, it is necessary to identify the type of object that unsafe.Pointer points to, which requires incorporating type inference and pointer analysis passes in the compiler. However, integrating current cmd/cgo, which handles CGO in the toolchain, with the type inference and pointer analysis passes of the Go compiler is a challenging task. It’s because: 1. Currently, the decision to insert cgoCheckPointer occurs at the AST representation stage, which is unsuitable for pointer analysis. 2. Currently, cmd/cgo exists as a standalone tool within the Go compila- tion toolchain rather than being part of the Go compiler itself. Therefore, integrating cmd/cgo into the compiler and enabling it to reuse the type inference and pointer analysis passes would require modifying the existing Go compilation process. This is a significant undertaking, and for broader applicability, it would require the involvement of the Go team. To address this, we propose a two-phase solution: 1. Initially, implementatemporarybuteffectiveapproachthatcanhandle most scenarios. 2. Submit a proposal to the Go team, hoping they will address the issue in the future. Internal Threats Sampling Bias. Ourfocusonpopularopen-sourceprojectsandkeyword- based issue searches may overlook patterns in less-known projects and under- estimate CGO’s challenges. To mitigate this, we clearly define our selection criteria, which deliberately scopes the study to active, popular projects. This ensuresourfindingsaregroundedininfluentialcommunitypracticesandoffer relevant insights for contemporary Go developers. Accuracy of Our Analysis Tools. A general, inherent limitation of static AST analysis is its inability to detect dynamic features. As CGOAna- lyzer relies on this technique, it may miss CGO calls generated dynamically or expanded from complex C macros, potentially leading to false negatives. To mitigate this, we built CGOAnalyzer atop Go’s official go/parser pack- age, which robustly handles the complexities of both Go and CGO code, ensuring broad applicability across projects. While dynamic analysis could capture such calls, it introduces other trade-offs and is beyond the scope of our large-scale static study. Subjectivity in Qualitative Analysis. The interpretation of issues such as compilation errors, bugs, and runtime crashes may be influenced by researchers’preconceivednotionsorbiases, leadingtosubjectiveassessments. External Threats The first external threat concerns generalizability. Our findings pertain specifically to popular open-source Go projects on GitHub and may not ex- tend to other Go projects hosted on different platforms, private projects, or those from specialized domains with fewer stars. Secondly, the study’s con- text within Go projects may overlook unique challenges or usage patterns 39 in projects using different development methodologies, limiting broader ap- plicability. Moreover, the usage of CGO is typically concentrated in a few spe- cific files or modules. Using CGO can enhance the flexibility and scalability of Go projects, and developers often use it to interact with the system and achieve better performance. JSON: Name: cgo_pointer_check_mitigation Title: Static and compiler-assisted analysis to identify and eliminate unnecessary cgo pointer checks in Go toolchain Short Hypothesis: A static analysis that (1) recognizes direct casts and address-taking patterns to unsafe.Pointer and (2) reuses compiler type and pointer-analysis results will significantly reduce the number of unnecessary cgoCheckPointer insertions and associated false-positive runtime panics without increasing the incidence of missed real pointer-safety violations. Related Work: Prior work has studied foreign-function interfaces (FFIs) in multiple ecosystems and developed static analyzers for Python/C and JNI, but these approaches do not account for Go-specific CGO preprocessing or Go runtime semantics. Existing tooling for Go includes ad-hoc analyzers and generator tools that create CGO bindings and some static checkers for unsafe usages; a single prior work focused on semi-automatic CGO binding generation. The Go toolchain currently implements conservative insertion of runtime pointer checks (cgoCheckPointer) during cmd/cgo preprocessing; many reported issues and patches show this conservative approach yields false positives and runtime panics. No existing approach both (a) applies targeted AST-level tracking for common safe cast patterns and (b) integrates compiler-level type/pointer-analysis passes to make check insertion precise. Limitations of current methods include lack of Go-specific pointer-flow modeling, absence of reuse of compiler analysis results by cmd/cgo, and reliance on either unsafe heuristics or heavy-weight full pointer analysis that has not been integrated into CGO preprocessing. Abstract: CGO enables interoperability between Go and C but the Go compilation toolchain conservatively inserts runtime pointer checks (cgoCheckPointer) for unsafe.Pointer usages, causing false-positive panics and undermining software reliability. We propose a two-tiered approach: a lightweight static AST-based analysis to detect common, provably-safe cast/address-taking patterns to unsafe.Pointer and suppress unnecessary checks; and a long-term compiler-integrated solution that reuses the compiler�s type inference and pointer-analysis passes to determine precise pointer targets during CGO preprocessing. Contributions include (1) a formal specification of cast/address-taking patterns that are safe to elide, (2) an evaluation on a large corpus of open-source Go projects demonstrating measurable reduction in unnecessary checks and avoided false panics, and (3) a design for integrating CGO preprocessing with compiler analyses to achieve sounder check placement. Expected outcomes are fewer spurious runtime panics, improved developer experience, and a clear roadmap for toolchain changes to resolve longstanding CGO pointer-check problems. Experiments: Datasets: (1) The filtered top-1000-star Go repositories (use the same filtering to produce 920 active repositories), (2) the 104 repositories identified with CGO usage, (3) a targeted set of 20 high-CGO-use repositories (bindings and system libraries) and (4) the official Go misc/cgo test suite and golang/go issue-driven testcases relevant to pointer checks. Baselines: (A) Unmodified Go toolchain (current cmd/cgo behavior), (B) the existing ad-hoc temporary heuristic used in the study (if available), (C) a disabled-check baseline (for safety measurement only). Proposed methods: (1) AST-based pattern recognizer that tracks unsafe.Pointer(expr) and unsafe.Pointer(&expr) to resolve expr type via AST and local declarations; (2) simulated compiler-integrated variant that uses full pointer-analysis results (where available). Metrics: percentage reduction in cgoCheckPointer insertions (Δchecks = 1 - removed/original), number of avoided false-positive panics (count of executions where baseline panics but method does not), safety regressions (count of real violations missed where method fails to insert a required check), precision and recall of removed-check classification (using manually labeled ground truth for sampled call-sites), build success rate, end-to-end test-suite pass rate, and added compile-time overhead (wall-clock). Experimental setup: run all repositories through (A),(B),(1),(2) with identical Go version and environment; capture preprocessing output and instrumented runtime behavior by executing existing unit/integration tests and curated reproducer inputs from issue reports. For ground truth, manually label a stratified random sample (n>=500) of cgo call-sites across repositories to determine whether check removal is safe. Ablation studies: (i) AST-only (case-tracking) vs AST+declaration-resolution, (ii) per-pattern ablation (only unsafe.Pointer(&expr) vs only unsafe.Pointer(expr)), (iii) effect of adding interprocedural local variable tracking, and (iv) simulated full pointer-analysis effect compared to AST-only. Statistical analysis: report mean and 95% confidence intervals across repositories and perform paired significance tests between baselines and methods for Δchecks and false-positive panic counts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Static unsoundness: the AST-based heuristic can miss aliasing, indirect flows, reflection, or generated code, producing false negatives that may fail to remove checks or, worse, incorrectly elide checks in unsafe scenarios. Ground-truth labeling: manual labeling for precision/recall is labor intensive and may introduce annotation bias. Scalability and compile-time cost: integrating full pointer analysis into preprocessing can increase compilation time and memory usage, challenging large codebases and CI pipelines. Platform variability: cross-compilation and platform-specific C libraries or different malloc implementations can change mspan layout and invalidate some heuristics. Language evolution: changes in Go�s compiler internals or CGO preprocessing pipeline may require repeated engineering work. Generalization limits: techniques tuned to common patterns (CString/free, memcpy, GoBytes) may not generalize to all libraries, embedded assembly, or complex C macros. Toolchain integration complexity: making cmd/cgo reuse compiler passes requires substantial refactoring and coordination with the Go project, which may delay adoption.
